A telamon is a sculpted figure of a man — carved from stone — that is used in place of a column or pillar to physically hold up part of a building. Instead of a plain, round column supporting a roof, a balcony, or a ledge above a doorway, the architect uses a human statue to do that job. The man-statue is the column.

Think of it this way: imagine a powerful man standing against a wall, arms raised and pressed upward, with the heavy stone ledge of a building resting directly on his head and hands. He looks like he's holding the building up. That is a telamon.

Telamons are almost always depicted as muscular, powerful men — because the whole visual point is to show strength bearing a great load. They are typically shown in one of a few poses:

  • Arms raised overhead, palms flat against the weight above
  • Bent slightly forward or at the knees, as if straining under pressure
  • Standing upright with the load bearing down on their head or shoulders

They are not decorative figures placed next to a column. They replace the column entirely. The statue itself is the load-bearing element (or at least appears to be — sometimes a hidden structural support does the real work behind the scenes, but visually, the man is doing the lifting).

In classical architecture, a column supports the horizontal beam or ledge above it — called an entablature. A telamon performs that exact same structural role, but instead of a plain stone cylinder, you get a sculpted human form. So wherever you would normally expect to see a column, you instead see one of these figures.

They appear:

  • Flanking grand doorways
  • Supporting balconies
  • Holding up the edges of a porch or portico
  • As part of a building's facade, evenly spaced like columns would be

The easiest way to sharpen your understanding of a telamon is to compare it to a caryatid.

A caryatid is exactly the same concept — a sculpted figure used as a column — except it is a female figure. The most famous examples in the world are the six graceful female figures on the Erechtheion temple on the Acropolis in Athens, Greece, each one elegantly supporting the porch roof on her head.

So the rule is simple:

  • Female figure used as a column → Caryatid
  • Male figure used as a column → Telamon

If you remember caryatids (which are more widely known), just think of a telamon as the male counterpart — and where a caryatid tends to look serene and upright, a telamon tends to look powerful, strained, and muscular, visually communicating the effort of bearing enormous weight.
Other Names for the Same Thing

A telamon is also commonly called an atlas (plural: atlantes). This name comes from the Greek god Atlas, who was condemned to hold up the sky on his shoulders for eternity — a perfect metaphor for a figure permanently frozen in stone, holding a building above its head. In many architecture books and museum descriptions, you will see the term "atlantes" used where another source might say "telamons." They mean the same thing.

So: telamon = atlas (as an architectural term). Both words are accepted and widely used.

Telamons have appeared across many periods of architectural history:

  • Ancient Greece and Rome: The earliest and most dramatic examples. The Temple of Olympian Zeus at Akragas (modern Agrigento, Sicily) featured enormous telamons — over 7 meters tall — integrated into its walls.
  • Renaissance and Baroque Europe: Architects revived the idea enthusiastically. You'll find telamons on palaces, civic buildings, and grand doorways across Italy, Austria, Germany, and France.
  • 19th-century neoclassical buildings: Banks, opera houses, and government buildings often used telamons as a way to project power and grandeur.

Today, if you visit any major museum of classical antiquities or walk through the historic centers of cities like Vienna, Rome, or Palermo, you are very likely to encounter them.

Unlike caryatids — which communicate elegance, grace, and calm — telamons are deliberately intense. The visual language is one of burden, effort, and submission to weight. The man is trapped, permanently straining. This makes them a powerful artistic and architectural choice: they don't just hold up a building, they dramatize the act of holding it up. Some scholars read them as symbols of conquered enemies forced to bear the weight of the victor's glory — which aligns with how some ancient civilizations used them as triumphant imagery.
A telamon is a sculpted stone figure of a muscular man that serves as a column in architecture, holding up a structure above it — the male equivalent of a caryatid, and also known as an atlas.
